verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, of David. Says [the] fool in his heart: "There-is-no God." They have acted corruptly, they have done abominably [in] deed; there is none doing good.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, a song of David. In the quiet of his own heart, where no one hears, the fool says it: "There is no God." And look at what follows from that silence. Lives gone rotten, deeds that turn the stomach, and not one person left who does good.
verses.directors_commentary:
Open on a whisper, not a shout. The fool speaks "in his heart", and in Hebrew the heart is the seat of the mind and the will, so this is a private decision, made where no one can contradict it. The word nabal does not mean 'stupid'. It means someone morally hollow, who has cut himself off from any accountability (it is also the name Abigail's husband carries in 1 Samuel 25, and he behaves as his name says). Play him as smug, not confused.

The KJV adds "is" and makes the line a philosophical proposition: "There is no God." The Hebrew is only 'ein elohim', 'no God', and the verses after it show what is meant. The fool does not argue that God is absent from the universe. He lives as though God neither sees nor judges, which is how Radak reads it: no judge, no justice, nobody to pay a man back for what he does. The BBE's "God will not do anything" catches this sense and loses the bluntness. Then the verse turns from the one man to a plural: "they" have acted corruptly, "they" have done abominably. Hebrew has the verbs in the perfect tense, as if the damage were already done.

The opening words, "to the choirmaster, of David", are part of verse 1 in the Hebrew, which is why the KJV numbers them 14:0. The ancient audience heard the title as a cue, a performance instruction: this is to be sung.

philological_notes.note: 'Fool' in the moral and religious sense, a person without regard for God or for others, and not an intellectual lack. The root also means to wither or fade, which gives the sense of someone who has wilted at the core. In Metzudat Zion the word is simply 'a low and mean person'.

Two verbs in the causative, one after the other, with no 'and': 'they have corrupted, they have made abominable [their] deed'. The causative suggests that the corruption is an action they carried out and chose, and not just a condition. 'Alilah' is a deed, with the sense of a doing that sets an example; Rashi glosses it with ma'alalim, 'deeds'.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH from heaven looks down upon the sons of Adam, to see: Is there one acting wisely, seeking [obj] God?
verses.translation_dramatic: But the LORD is watching. From heaven he leans out and looks down on the children of men, searching the faces of every one of them, asking one question: is there anyone here with sense, anyone who is looking for God?
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene lifts. After the whisper of a man's heart comes the view from above, and it should feel like a camera rising out of a courtyard into the sky. The verb hishqif is 'to bend over and look down', as someone does from a window or a rooftop. It makes the LORD attentive and close, even though he is in heaven. Radak says it plainly: he is high above them and hidden from their eyes, yet he looks at them and takes notice.

The KJV's "children of men" is a literal rendering of 'bene adam', and it is right to be literal: the phrase marks humans as earthbound, formed from the ground (adam from adamah), and set against the God who looks from heaven. Meiri adds that the psalm calls them this because of their folly. The KJV softens the two questions he asks by turning them into "any that did understand, and seek God", with a past tense and an 'and'. The Hebrew has two participles side by side, with no 'and': a 'one acting wisely', a 'one seeking God'. In this psalm wisdom and seeking are the same act. A maskil is not clever but someone whose insight shows in how he lives, and 'seeking God' (doresh) means turning to him for guidance, as one goes to an oracle. The divine name changes here, too: the fool said Elohim, but it is YHWH who looks. Hold a beat before the name.

philological_notes.note: To look down from a height, to peer out through a window or over a wall. Metzudat Zion defines it as 'a looking' (hatbaah). It is used of God to say that he sees from above, close up.
One who acts with insight, a person whose understanding results in right action. Metzudat David reads it as someone who will 'protest' (limchot) the evil, so understanding is shown in what one does.

verses.translation_literal: The whole [of it] has turned aside; together they are befouled. There is none doing good; there is not even one.
verses.translation_dramatic: Nothing. The answer comes back from every direction: all of them have turned off the road, and all together they have gone sour. No one who does good. Not one. Not even one.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the answer to the question of verse 2, and it should come flat, almost as an accounting. The grammar is a sweep: ha-kol, 'the whole', then yachdav, 'together', then 'not even one'. Three times the verse closes any exit. For sar, 'turned aside', as one leaves a path, Ibn Ezra says 'from the straight road', Radak 'from the way of the good', and Metzudat David 'from the way of the good': all of them left the road. Rashi hears a sharper charge: no man in the army, among the oppressors' own forces, raises a hand to protest. Either way the exits are closed.

The verb nealachu is the surprise. It occurs only here, in the parallel psalm and in Job 15:16, and the KJV smooths it into "filthy". Radak and Meiri connect it to chelah, the scum in Ezekiel's cooking pot (Ezek 24:6), by reversal of letters, and Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'stinking', as in Job 15:16. So hear a smell in the word. The KJV "no, not one" adds a comma that Hebrew does not have. The Hebrew says 'ein gam echad': 'there is not also one', a stammer that has the sense of 'not even one'; Ibn Ezra compares gam in Prov 14:20. The apostle Paul will quote this verse in Romans 3, but at this point the psalm is talking about the fool and his circle, the enemies of the poor in verse 6, and the actors should not play it as a statement about all humankind in every age.

philological_notes.note: 'Has turned aside', as from a path. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David all say the road is the straight or good way. Rashi reads the verse differently: no one in the army protests. Radak also records a variant reading, sag, 'turned back' (cf. Ps 53:4).

'They are befouled, spoiled'. A rare verb (also Job 15:16 and Ps 53:4) of moral corruption with an image of something rotten. Ibn Ezra glosses it 'like nishchatu', 'they are corrupted'. Radak and Meiri connect it with chelah, 'scum', by reversal of letters.
'Not even one'. Metzudat Zion says that gam has the sense of 'even' (afilu), here to cut off the possibility of a single exception.

verses.translation_literal: Do they not know, all workers of iniquity, eaters of my people? They eat bread; YHWH they do not call.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do they not know, all those who work wickedness? They devour my people as if it were nothing more than a meal, tearing off a mouthful, and then another. And the LORD? They never call his name.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new voice breaks in: "my people". Whoever speaks here, God or the psalmist, it is the voice of someone who has been hurt in his own family, and the first word, halo, 'do they not know?', is not a question that expects an answer. Radak calls it an exclamation of astonishment: how can they all be so senseless? Play it as a throat tightening.

The hard clause is akhelu lechem, 'they eat bread', which the KJV makes a comparison: "as they eat bread". The English reads smoothly, but the Hebrew has no 'as'. Two ways to hear it, and the commentators split. Most take it as a simile: the meal is the picture of how casually they devour the people (Radak: 'they eat my people as they eat the bread'; Ibn Ezra: 'while they ate my people as if they ate bread'; Meiri: they swallow Israel like a delicacy). Rashi alone hears a separate accusation: they sat down to a feast, and he cites Belshazzar's banquet (Dan 5:1), without a thought for God. Malbim goes his own way: 'they ate bread' refers to Israel, who ate without blessing God and so were afraid of punishment, in contrast with these men who do not fear at all. The ambiguity is useful for an actor. They eat my people; they eat their bread; neither meal is preceded by a word to God. That is why the last clause is YHWH 'lo qara'u', 'they do not call [him]', and the name sits in front of the verb for emphasis.

The verb 'eat' for oppression is a standard image of an economy in which the strong live off the poor: taxes, debt, seized fields. 'Workers of iniquity' (poale aven) are not secret sinners but those whose work is making others suffer.

philological_notes.note: 'Eaters of my people', 'eat' as a figure for violent exploitation. The following 'they eat bread' is read as the simile (they eat my people as one eats bread) by Radak, Ibn Ezra and Meiri, and by Rashi as a separate statement about a feast. Malbim refers it to Israel eating without blessing God.

'They have not called [on him]': they do not pray to him and do not acknowledge him. Radak records three readings: it did not occur to them that YHWH sees; they thought themselves safe because they had not been punished; they stay in their evil and do not repent. Meiri reads it as not blessing God at their meals.

verses.translation_literal: There they feared a fear, for God [is] with a righteous generation.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then, there, terror. Dread takes hold of them and will not let go. For God is with the righteous generation, and they have run into him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns on one word, sham, 'there'. It points at a place or a moment, and the text does not say which: the commentators put it in Jerusalem, at the feast, at the scene of the oppression. The KJV's "There were they in great fear" turns a vivid image into a plain description. The Hebrew says 'they feared a fear': pachadu pachad, the verb and its own noun together, the way Hebrew makes something total. Say it so the sound repeats, with the plosive p and the throat of the ch: pa-cha-du pa-chad. The fear is not mild; it is a seizure.

The reason follows with ki: God is 'in' (be-) the righteous generation, that is, with them as a presence, as a defender. The KJV "in the generation of the righteous" suggests a place; "with" is closer. Ibn Ezra compares 'to the help of YHWH among the mighty': God stands with those who are being devoured. Note that dor tsaddiq is singular, 'a righteous generation', and not 'the generation of the righteous'; the KJV adds the definite article that the Hebrew lacks. The victims of verse 4 are not named righteous because they are perfect, but because of the side God takes.

philological_notes.note: A verb with its own noun (cognate accusative): 'they feared a fear', 'they were in terror'. The sound repeats in the Hebrew. Radak notes that the past tense stands for the future, 'they will fear'.

'With/in a righteous generation'. Without the definite article, and the be- is 'with' (on the side of). Rashi applies it to the generation of Jeconiah; Meiri to Daniel and his companions; Metzudat David to a generation in which God was present, in contrast with the later wicked ones.

verses.translation_literal: The counsel of [the] poor you put to shame, for YHWH [is] his refuge.
verses.translation_dramatic: You laugh at the plans of the poor. You make them blush for trusting. But the LORD is his refuge.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker turns on the oppressors and speaks to them directly: tavishu, 'you put to shame'. It is the only verse in the psalm in the second person, and the shift should feel like a door opening. The target of their mockery is the 'atsat ani', the poor man's 'counsel': his plan, and his intention. He has no army and no silver, and his whole strategy is that YHWH is his refuge. Rashi and Metzudat David say it exactly: you mock them because they trust in the LORD, or because they say 'YHWH is my refuge'. The oppressors' joke is the one Radak quotes from Deuteronomy 32:37: 'Where is their God? Let him rise and help you.'

The KJV's "Ye have shamed" is a perfect-tense past, but the Hebrew form is imperfect: you keep shaming, you go on shaming. The YLT's "cause to stink" confuses bush, 'be ashamed', with another verb, ba'ash, 'to stink', and the BBE's "thoughts" loses the weight of 'atsah as a practical plan. In ancient Near Eastern thinking a poor man (ani) was someone with no legal power: no land, no patron, no protection in the gate. A machseh, 'refuge', is a physical shelter, a rock or a cave to run to in a storm. His only patron is God.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of בוש, 'to put to shame, to make blush'. Rashi has them say that the poor man's plan is a disgrace; Meiri reads it as 'you make his plan a disappointed one that returns empty'.
'His refuge', a shelter to flee into (root חסה, to take refuge). Radak: it is his only plan, because 'he has no other refuge'.

verses.translation_literal: Who will give from Zion the deliverance of Israel? In the turning back of YHWH [to] the captivity of his people, Jacob will rejoice, Israel will be glad.
verses.translation_dramatic: Oh, who will send it out of Zion, the rescue of Israel? When the LORD turns back and brings his people home from captivity, then Jacob will cry out for joy, and Israel will be glad.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends in a sigh that turns into a song. Mi yitten, literally 'who will give?', is the idiom for a wish: 'if only', 'would that'. Meiri has an alternative, that it is a rhetorical question, 'who is it that gives deliverance from Zion?', but most read it as a longing. Let the voice rise on 'Zion', the place where the LORD's presence lived in the temple, the source from which Radak says help must come.

The KJV "Oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion!" renders the wish well, but "bringeth back the captivity" hides a wordplay. The idiom is shuv shevut, and the root shuv ('to return') sounds twice, in beshuv ('when [he] turns') and, close enough to hear, in shevut. Radak reads beshuv first as transitive, 'in bringing back' (like behashiv), and gives as an alternative 'in the quieting' (from beshuvah vanachat, Isa 30:15); Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion read only 'quieting': when the LORD calms his people. The phrase can mean 'bring home the captives' or, more broadly, 'restore the fortunes', and the Hebrew does not pick.

The last line is a pair: Jacob rejoices, Israel is glad. These are one people under two names, said in parallel to make it sound like a chorus. Yagel is jussive in form, 'let Jacob rejoice'; yismach has the shape of an ordinary imperfect and can be read either way, so the English 'will' in the literal layer and 'let' in this commentary are both inside what the Hebrew allows. The tone is that of a prayer. This is what the poor man's refuge was for.

philological_notes.note: Either transitive, 'in bringing back' (Radak's first reading, like behashiv), or 'in the quieting' (Isa 30:15), which is the only reading of Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion and Radak's second.
'Captivity' (Metzudat Zion links it with shevi, captivity); in the idiom shuv shevut it can be broader, 'fortunes'.
A fixed wish-formula, 'who will give?' = 'would that'. Metzudat David reads it as 'let it come quickly'. Meiri takes it as a rhetorical question and not a prayer.
A parallel pair. The first verb is jussive in form ('let Jacob rejoice'); the second has the imperfect form and can be read either way.
